subject: Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)

messages.author: 52490181456ca7ea
messages.subject: Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
parts:
Hey guys,
Sorry if this doesn't belong on this mailing list. I just couldn't find a better place to ask the question

I'm wondering if anyone of you could tell me any real difference and/or advantage to the following two methods of partial pooling in those simple regression models.

1. example.
For each response variable y_k, (where k = (1:N), each k could e.g. be a different school or country), we want to model the effect of data x on the data y_k, by sampling B_k and an intercept B_0. Assuming all y's are related we pool the B_k towards each other by sampling the mean of each B_k from the same hyper prior. Thus the sigma in b) says how much each B_k are allowed to vary from each other but the sigma_hat in c) determines the width of the over all prior distribution of the effect. 

a) y_k ~ x *B_k + B_0

b) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)

c) mu ~ N(mu_hat,sigma_hat)


2. Here the individual B_k's would be effects of each individual model, but they are multiplied with a completely pooled, shared parameter A which is the same parameter for all the different models. Thus the sigma will say how much the B_k's can vary from each other and then the A will determine the over all effect.

aa)  y_k ~ x *A*B_k + B_0

bb) B_k ~ N(mu, sigma)

cc) A ~ N(mu_hat, sigma_hat)


Now the equations are different, but the design of the models are supposed to work in the same way.
But do they? Can we implement some sort of a matt-trick for the second version? And btw I can see how correlations may be very troublesome between all the B_k's and the A in the second case. 

Best regards,
Jökull Snæbjarnarson

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
parts:
In the future be careful with hats — in statistics they are usually
reserved for estimators which are functions of the data and not
hyperparameters.  For example, less than careful reading of this 
post by a statistician could easily be confused for something like 
an empirical Bayes approximation where you plug in data estimates 
for hyperpriors.

Notation aside, (1) and (2) are not equivalent.  Firstly, mu and sigma
always need priors, so even if you introduce A in (2) then you still
need to define a prior for mu or you haven’t fully specified your model.

More importantly, mu has the effect of translating the B_k, not scaling
them.  This is easier to see if you write (1) with a non-centered parameterization,

y_{k} ~ N( x * (mu + sigma * B_k) + B_{0}, upsilon)
B_k ~ N(0, 1)
// hyperpriors for mu, sigma, and upsilon

mu just shifts the overall effect, while sigma is responsible for scaling
the individual effects.  So if you introduced an A that multiplies x then
you would be affecting the variance of the population.

If you’re careful then you could manipulate this into an equivalent model,
but then you’d have a non-identifiability between A and sigma.  In other
words, you’re just replacing alpha by (alpha_{1} + alpha_{2}) which is
technically valid but will make the model much harder to fit for no good
reason.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Two ways of hierarchical pooling (warning it's more of a math discussion, than stan)
parts:
The whole point of a hierarchical model is to let
sigma (and mu) be a parameter and learn it from
the population data!  Uniform priors, however, put
way too much probability at high values of B/sigma
where there is no pooling of the B at all.
On May 26, 2016, at 1:39 PM, Jökull Snæbjarnarson <jok...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks for the reply, I'll try to be more careful with the hats :) 

And ok yes I get the non-identifiability.

But I think i'm lacking some understanding of the need for a prior of the sigma. Could you explain or point me towards some literature? 
Is there difference of the distribution of B in this case:

y ~ x*B+B0
B ~ uniform[0,inf]

and

y ~ x*B+B0
B~ N(0,sigma)
sigma ~ uniform[0,inf]

-Jökull
